references.text: Matthew's parallel account of Jesus casting out a mute demon, where the crowd is amazed and the Pharisees accuse him of driving out demons by Beelzebul.
Matthew's account of the healing of a blind and mute man possessed by a demon, followed by the crowd's amazement and the Pharisees' accusation of Beelzebul—a close parallel to Luke 11:14-15.
Mark's account where the scribes accuse Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, which is the same controversy that follows Luke 11:14.
The crowd marvels at Jesus' deeds and says he does all things well—he makes both the deaf hear and the mute speak. This reflects the crowd's reaction in Luke 11:14.
It mentions that people brought to Jesus all who were suffering from various diseases, including those possessed by demons, and he healed them—showing Jesus' general power over demons.
Isaiah's prophecy that the tongue of the mute shall shout for joy when God comes to save, a messianic prophecy that Jesus fulfills when he heals the mute man.
The immediate continuation where some of the listeners accuse Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons—the controversy triggered by this healing.
A previous example in Luke where Jesus casts out an unclean spirit and the crowd is amazed, illustrating the recurring pattern of Jesus' exorcisms and the people's reaction.
Jesus points to his miracles—including that the blind see and the mute speak—as proof that he is the one who was to come, confirming the messianic significance of the healing in 11:14.
